issues.explanation: The threat items suggest an interpersonal/physical attack context ('sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard', needing to stay alert at night for danger) rather than a child illness trauma. For a parent's trauma involving a child's illness, threat is more typically about recurrence, medical crises, or inability to protect the child, not immediate guarding against others' movements.

issues.explanation: 'What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it' implies a perpetrator, negligence, or unresolved external wrongdoing. That appraisal can occur after medical trauma, but in this profile there are no memory, trigger, or threat items indicating medical error, institutional betrayal, or blame context, so it sits awkwardly with the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Pregnancy/birth/babies reminders are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness. For this trauma type, child-health, hospital, medical, or illness-related cues would be expected; pregnancy/childbirth cues imply a different trauma context unless there is additional undisclosed perinatal trauma.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
issues.explanation: The appraisal that 'nothing has been done about it' fits neglect, betrayal, or preventable harm more than a child's serious illness. In the context of a life-threatening illness, the unfairness element is plausible, but the added idea that nothing has been done is clinically discordant unless there was clear medical negligence, which is not otherwise reflected in the profile.

Alcohol smell is not well aligned with the stated trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, while the other trigger items are strongly medical/hospital-based. Without any corroborating trauma content suggesting alcohol was central to the child's illness experience, this item looks clinically out of place within the trigger set.

issues.item: Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
issues.explanation: 'Cannot trust safety' suggests a pervasive current danger appraisal more typical of interpersonal violence, combat, or repeated external threat. For a trauma centered on a child's life-threatening illness, this can occur, but here it is not well supported by the rest of the profile, which is focused on medical reminders and reliving rather than generalized danger.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: Sleep vigilance because one 'need[s] to stay alert' implies ongoing monitoring for imminent threat. In the context of a child's past life-threatening illness, this is difficult to reconcile unless there is corresponding material about night-time monitoring, medical deterioration, or responsibility for detecting danger, which is absent from the selected items.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: The hospital/medical trigger pattern fits a child's life-threatening illness, but a burnt-smell danger cue is hard to reconcile with that trauma context unless there is specific unreported trauma-related meaning. As selected, it stands out as clinically implausible relative to the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
issues.explanation: The olfactory memory item implies the original trauma involved a distinctive smell that is re-experienced. In this profile, the only corroborating smell tied to the trauma context should be hospital/antiseptic cues; pairing it with a burnt-smell trigger creates an incoherent sensory trauma context for a child's medical illness.

vignette:
Arun had been a bomb disposal technician for over thirty years, a man whose entire professional identity was built on the ability to stay calm under pressure, to assess and neutralize threats with deliberate, surgical precision. He had dismantled improvised explosive devices in cramped basements and crowded streets, always trusting his training and his hands. But nothing in his career had prepared him for the day his five-year-old son Ravi was rushed to the emergency room with a sky-high fever and a stiff neck. The diagnosis came fast: bacterial meningitis. For two weeks, Arun sat in a plastic chair beside a hospital bed, watching his son slip in and out of consciousness while monitors beeped and drips delivered fluids into a small, still arm. He could not defuse this. He could not even slow it down.

Ravi eventually recovered, fully and without complications, but something in Arun had not come back. The first time he noticed it was a few weeks after discharge, when he walked past a janitor mopping the floor of his local grocery store. The smell of antiseptic—bleach and something sterile—hit him without warning, and he was suddenly back in that hospital room, the fluorescent lights humming, the sharp odour of hand sanitiser coating his skin. His heart pounded, his palms went slick, and for a few seconds he forgot where he was. He told himself it was just a stray memory, but the same thing happened again a week later when he saw a discarded syringe in a carpark. The image of the drip needle in Ravi’s arm flashed across his mind, full-colour and total, and he felt the same helpless dread he had felt watching the doctors work. He began to realise that the memory did not need permission to arrive. It came on its own schedule, triggered by the most ordinary things.

At home, he started avoiding certain rooms. The small bathroom cabinet held plasters and an old thermometer, and he kept the door closed. His wife noticed he stopped volunteering to take Ravi to check-ups. He gave vague excuses about work, but the real reason was that he could no longer stand the sight of a stethoscope or the sound of a paediatrician’s cheerful voice over the hum of an air-conditioner. Over time, his avoidance widened. He found himself uncomfortable around children generally—neighbourhood kids playing in the street, his own nephews at family gatherings. Their high voices and sudden movements reminded him of Ravi in the hospital bed, and he felt a surge of fear he could not explain. He began to excuse himself early from dinners, claiming exhaustion.

Sleep became a battleground. At night, lying beside his wife, Arun could not let his vigilance drop. He needed to stay alert, as if some threat might creep in while he was defenceless. He would lie awake for hours, listening to the house settle, braced for nothing in particular but unable to unclench his jaw. His body reacted to every slight sound—a floorboard creak, a distant siren—with a jolt of adrenaline that made his heart hammer and his hands shake. He told himself this was reasonable, that he was just being careful, but a quieter voice inside him whispered that he was falling apart. He began to believe that his reactions meant he was losing his mind. How else could a grown man, a bomb technician, be undone by the smell of a cleaning product? He felt weak, fundamentally flawed. The same man who had walked calmly toward live explosives now flinched at a child’s laugh.

At work, the consequences crept in. During a routine disposal of an old military ordnance, he noticed a first-aid kit lying nearby in the blast zone. The white cross on the red background triggered the image of a hospital wristband, and he froze for a full five seconds before his partner’s voice brought him back. He managed to complete the operation, but the lapse terrified him. He started double-checking his own equipment obsessively, aware that his concentration was fraying. He requested reassignment from night shifts, telling his supervisor it was for family reasons, but privately he knew the truth: he was afraid that one more sudden memory would cost him his focus at the wrong moment.

What finally brought him to seek help was not his own fear but his wife’s gentle insistence after he recoiled from holding his new grandson. The baby was sleeping in his mother’s arms, a tiny bundle, and Arun’s chest seized with an irrational terror that the child was too still, too quiet. He pulled his hands back as if burned. That night, he sat in the dark living room and admitted to himself that he could not continue like this. He wanted to feel steady again. He wanted to hold his grandson without the taste of antiseptic in his mouth. But he was terrified that talking about it would only confirm what he already suspected—that he was broken in a way that no amount of training could fix.
